title: Gordon Street development approved amid traffic concerns
subtitle: Habitat for Humanity Speedvale apartment proposal received, plus a pedestrian crosswalk study near Lansdown Road.
overview: Council approved Official Plan and zoning changes for 1166-1204 Gordon Street, allowing two six-storey apartment buildings with 122 units and 20 three-storey townhouses {{vote:m3}}. Staff recommended approval, and council noted the revised plan was improved from the original and met the zoning by-law's parking requirements.

Residents who spoke were not opposed to development. They raised concerns about traffic, turning onto Gordon Street, school bus stops and pedestrian safety on and near Lansdown Drive. In response, council directed staff to study whether a pedestrian crosswalk is warranted on Gordon Street near Lansdown Road by the end of Q4 2024 {{vote:m4}}.

Council also received a statutory public meeting report on a proposed six-storey, 48-unit Habitat for Humanity apartment building at 303-317 Speedvale Avenue East {{vote:m2}}. No decision was made. Staff expect to bring it back in September, and residents raised concerns about flooding, parking and the number of requested zoning exceptions.

decisions.detail: Council approved the Official Plan and zoning by-law amendments for two six-storey apartment buildings (122 units) and 20 three-storey on-street townhouses, with no further public notice required.
Staff will study the warrants for a pedestrian crosswalk on Gordon Street near Lansdown Road by the end of Q4 2024.
Council received the statutory public meeting report on the proposed six-storey, 48-unit apartment building; no decision was made and the application returns to council later.

debate: Delegates on the Gordon Street proposal said Lansdown Drive is narrow and serves about 64 homes. They worried about added traffic, hard left turns onto Gordon Street without lights, a steep icy stretch of Valley Road, and school bus stops near the new driveways.

Delegates asked that the apartment buildings not use Lansdown Drive for access, and asked for a fuller traffic study and measures such as traffic lights or a crossing. Staff said access directly onto Gordon Street is not supported, and that Lansdown Drive is a local road with capacity for the added traffic.

Staff said a future Lansdown extension to Edinburgh Road with a signalised intersection is preferred, but it depends on a separate appeal before the Ontario Land Tribunal. Staff said signals and crossings are assessed through warrant analysis.

One councillor said the Gordon Street proposal was deficient in massing and traffic and in its site-specific zoning. Staff said it needs no special height or step-back exceptions, and other councillors said it was much improved and met zoning rules, and that refusal risked an appeal to the tribunal.

At the Speedvale meeting, a neighbour questioned the 14 requested zoning exceptions, parking, and stormwater and flooding on nearby streets, and said six storeys is too big for the lot. The applicant and staff pointed to servicing and stormwater studies. Councillors asked about the reduced amenity space, zero parking setbacks and the unit mix.
